paras: The lynching of William Lewis was the hanging of a Black man by unknown persons near Durant, Mississippi, whose body was found on a tree on the morning of September 4, 1888. No cause was assigned and the perpetrators were not identified. The case reached readers only as a brief wire item, printed in Savannah and in several Northern papers the next day.

According to a dispatch from Durant relayed through New Orleans, the body of William Lewis, described as "colored," was discovered hanging to a tree five miles from the town on the morning of September 4. The correspondent judged that he had "evidently" been hanged the night before. The dispatch stated that the perpetrators were unknown and that "No cause is assigned." A shorter version of the wire, dated September 5, said only that Lewis was "supposed to have been lynched by unknown persons."
No report of an inquest, an arrest, or any official response appears in the coverage, and no later account of the case was found.

Every report found came from white newspapers on September 5, 1888, and all of them rest on the single Durant dispatch. The Savannah Morning News printed the fullest text under the headline "A Negro Found Hanged," quoting the correspondent without comment. The Evening Journal and the Waterbury Evening Democrat ran the shorter version under the headline "Lynched Very Quietly." The Daily Republican reduced the case to one sentence in its news summary, placed among drownings and suicides, ending "The lynchers are unknown."
None of the papers named an accusation against Lewis, and none offered editorial comment on the killing.

reader.title: Lynching of William Lewis
bases: A Black man was found hanged from a tree near Durant and the wire reports said he was lynched by unknown persons (A1, A2, A3).

Lewis was found hanged and the reports attribute the killing to unknown 'lynchers' (A1, A2), but no account gives the number of perpetrators, and the Durant dispatch says 'No cause is assigned' (A3), so the group size and the pretext are not reported.
All versions trace to one New Orleans relay of a Durant dispatch, printed in fuller (A3) and shorter (A2, A4) forms and summarized in A1; no independent local or second account was found.
